Just to clarify, Valen's borrow checker can express shared-xor-mutable, its value proposition is that it can _also_ express mutable aliasing (with `in`).

* When a function has a mutable effect into a group, and the function doesn't declare any other groups to alias it (with `in`), it is effectively a unique reference.

* When a function has references into a group, and it declares no `mut` effects into any of them, they are effectively shared/immutable references.

This helps with Valen's structured concurrency in particular, but also helps guard against the single-threaded race conditions in the same way that Rust's borrow checker does. It also helps with Rust interop!

So, TL;DR: Valen lets you choose between shared-xor-mutable and mutable aliasing.

Also note how mutable aliasing is opt-in (via `in`), so there's a subtle influence pushing people towards shared-xor-mutable, so that they only reach for mutable aliasing when it will benefit them.

Short answer: Valen would have something similar to Fn and FnMut (but phrased in terms of effects rather than Fn vs FnMut). In other words, we would be able to express "a closure that does not modify anything it captures", or rather, "a closure that has no mut effects".

That closure, because it doesn't modify anything it captures, would be safe to share among multiple threads in a structured-concurrency-like / std::thread::scope-ish way.

The key here is that one _can_ express immutable references in Valen; an immutable reference is a reference that the containing function doesn't express a `mut` effect for. And once we have immutable references, we get all of the nice concurrency benefits that Rust trailblazed.

To add onto this: it is generally not possible for suppliers to sell below market rate. If DDR5 is going for $400/16GB, and you want to sell 16GB for $200, people are going to buy your cheap RAM until you run out and resell it for more money. This is called arbitrage, and it's the market rewarding others for being greedy where you weren't. The only way to make the price go down is to make the market's price go down: produce so much supply that you extinguish all of the arbitrage-driven demand.

There are some wrinkles to this. If CXMT's RAM was somehow inferior, then the market could sustain two different prices for two different products. But it's difficult to separate the market like this without just making unusable trash. The one separation we do have - DDR5 vs HBM - works against the consumer's favor. One layer down in the supply chain, RAM manufacturers have to buy silicon wafers to etch circuits into, and HBM takes up treble more wafer space than DDR5 per gigabyte. In fact, this is specifically the scarcity that allowed Sam Altman to engineer a RAM crisis, by buying up a bunch of wafer supply that he could then redirect to more AI-optimized HBM.

We can also infer from all of this that CXMT - while producing lots of memory - does not have the scale necessary to actually quench the inflated demand. Either because their yields are shit, or because China wants to run a business and made the same calculation as the other RAM producers that the AI bubble would pop before they could get additional equipment online to service demand.

I built Vocafy, a music player web app for Vocaloid songs. You pick songs by producer, singer (voicebank), or year, and it plays the original videos from YouTube and Niconico.

Around 2010-2012, at the peak of the Vocaloid boom, I made music videos for a Vocaloid producer. I skipped university for days to edit videos, and it was honestly the most fulfilling time of my life. Lately Vocaloid songs seem to be showing up on YouTube again, so I thought now was the time to give something back. I built it together with Claude Code.

In my opinion, Vocaloid is mainly about the songs, not the videos. But there aren't many services focused on the songs. YouTube and Niconico are video services. YouTube Music mixes covers and unauthorized reuploads in with the originals, and its search isn't great, so it's hard to reach the song you want among the huge number of Vocaloid songs.

Features:

- Browse by voicebank, year, or producer

- Favorite songs and producers (sign in with Google to sync across devices)

- Continuous play, shuffle, and radio

- A picture-in-picture-like mini player

- Sleep timer

- Both YouTube and Niconico

- Add to home screen to use it as an app (Android, iOS, PC)

- Theme colors based on Vocaloid characters

Because of technical limits, background playback and continuous Niconico playback on iOS Safari are hard to support.

As of October 2026 there are about 30,000 songs, 800 producers, and 700 singers, and I add more every week. It's completely free. If a song you're looking for is missing, let me know.

Gubrud (1997), first recorded use: "By advanced artificial general intelligence, I mean AI systems that rival or surpass the human brain in complexity and speed ... " Modern LLMs completely blow us out of the water on speed and this has been true for over a year now. As for "complexity", we will forgive Gubrud, but that isn't really a meaningful concept. That said, the biggest modern LLMs are probably comparable to human brains in complexity at the level of analogizing synapse counts to parameter counts. Whether this is the right lens is up for debate.

Goertzel, Journal of AGI review (2014): AGI is a field building “general-purpose systems with intelligence comparable to that of the human mind.” Any leading model satisfies this definition easily, if only because "comparable" is a loose term. If modern LLMs can substitute for any expert in a knowledge work field and even directly teleoperate robots to perform complex tasks without prior training, that already sounds more than "comparable."

MIRI / Muehlhauser (2013): “the ability to achieve complex goals in complex environments using limited computational resources ... ” Well, I don't like this definition at all, but modern LLMs do satisfy it. They may be relatively inefficient in the training phase but they're incredibly efficient in the inference phase. (By "efficient" of course I mean information-efficient, not energy-efficient; this is surely the sense in which the definition was meant.)

Wikipedia in ~2016: “Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is the intelligence of a machine that could successfully perform any intellectual task that a human being can.” This is the most demanding definition of the bunch. But still, are there really any remaining intellectual tasks that cutting edge models can't achieve? If you think that you have an example one - are you sure it isn't just an example of a thing that nobody has bothered to ask, or bothered put a lot of compute behind? The operative concept here is could successfully perform, without regard for compute requirements. This may sound weaselly, but it is extremely relevant. To my mind, the question of "is it AGI or not" is about raw capabilities, not efficiency. Nobody writing sci-fi in the 2000s would have cared too much about the compute requirements of their speculative tech. In fact, a common trope was something like a gigantic mainframe that could be asked one question at a time. The modern instantiation of a gigantic mainframe that can hold 10 million parallel conversations was barely dreamed of.

Ldaxr works on any Aarch64 CPUs, but on Armv8.2-A and later CPUs, i.e. Cortex-A75, Cortex-A55 and all later CPUs, it is better to not use the non-deterministic ldaxr but to implement mutual exclusion and dynamic partitioning of shared resources using the fetch-and-add (ARM mnemonic LDADD) and fetch-and-store (a.k.a. atomic exchange a.k.a. atomic swap) (ARM mnemonic SWP) instructions, which can provide deterministic and fair behavior.

Also for shared bitmaps, which are useful in many algorithms, bits can be set and reset atomically with fetch-and-and-with-complement (ARM mnemonic LDCLR) or fetch-and-or (ARM mnemonic LDSET) instructions.

While for mutual exclusion or dynamic partitioning ldaxr is always a bad choice, in theory there are some algorithms for optimistic access to shared resources (a.k.a. lock-free) that can benefit from ldaxr, but even for optimistic access the most useful case is that of optimistic read-only access, which does not need ldaxr.

The fact that the first version of Aarch64 did not have anything else for implementing atomic accesses except ldaxr, was its biggest mistake, which was corrected quickly in Armv8.1-A and the CPUs with an ISA older than Armv8.2-A, i.e. Cortex-A72 and Cortex-A53, have been obsolete for almost a decade (though annoyingly one can find even today some embedded computers with such archaic CPU cores, which force the use of inefficient algorithms in multithreaded applications).

After reading multuple discussions in this thread and a bunch of others, I feel like people on HN think about art skills in the same way as they think of their software skills.

Correct me if I'm wrong, but skills that allowed one to make software largely made one pretty employable in the last few decades.

Now, art skills do not make you employable. There are narrow industries where you can make money but throughout the entirety of human history, being an artist rarely provided any sort of economic security. Some artists did and do make money. Sometimes it was prestigious but the barrier of entry was insanely high. And yes, getting to their level of skill and sometimes even getting access to the tools (look up how much a decent harp costs) was yet another enormous obstacle. Out of the entire pool of people who had artistic abilities, very few got access to tools and resources to be able to express their abilities. Out of those, even fewer could make money off of it while also doing artistic work that was deeply fulfilling and aligned with their talent. Occasionally, the stars would align and you would be lucky to be born in a time and place where you could get the schooling, the tools, the job that paid well enough and that didn't makwe your soul die because it alined with your natural creativity.

There are a lot of people who (I think) speak of AI as if democratizes access to the tools and therefore in their mind it should follow that there must be some market for their newlyfound creative expression. But if you ever seriously considered art as a career, you know that you will likely not have a market for your skills. It is difficult to make money even as a traditonal artist (as in a painter) or, say, a musician, god help you if you want to do mixed media, if you want to play avant garde jazz, prog rock, or Barocco music, if you want to be an actor, a playwright or a ballet dancer.

Some people (I assume those who are excited about the idea of being able to express themselves) seem to be bummed that the world rejects AI art as 'slop'. I am not going to say anything about effort, laziness, etc, I believe anything can be used to make art, even a toilet put in an exhibition hall (I like Duchamp, I like modern art, I like post-modern art, I like whatever-the-paradigm-we're-in-now-art -- metamodernism? I love art, I did see early pre-ChatGPT experiments with neural networks that moved me), but I have to say something that any aspiring artist must know -- you will not make money off your art. The people who will be making the 'human premium' that the article talks about, will be few, just like there are few of them now. AI artists will not make money of their art. Art is a terrible career choice, now and tomorrow.

It's still worth pursuing, in my opinion (as I said -- I love art), but there is little point of talking about its commercial viability. It will always be shit.
